summary: Jeremiah 21 (14 verses) continues the story of judgment. Starting with 'The word which came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur the son of Malchijah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest, saying,', it moves through themes of judgment, new covenant and calls readers toward tears.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows judgment lived out in jerusalem falling. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: The word which came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur the son of Malchijah, and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest, saying,
“You shall say to this people, ‘Yahweh says: “Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death.
I will punish you according to the fruit of your doings,’ says Yahweh; ‘and I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it will devour all that is around her.’”

questions.question: What is happening in Jeremiah 21?
questions.answer: In 14 verses, this chapter jeremiah 21 (14 verses) continues the story of judgment. starting with 'the word which came to jeremiah from yahweh, when king zedekiah sent to him pashhur the son of malchijah, and zephaniah the son of maaseiah, the priest, saying,', it moves through themes of judgment, new covenant and calls readers toward tears. The setting is jerusalem falling, written to judah before exile. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Jeremiah and why 21 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally jeremiah, addressed to judah before exile around ~600 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as prophetic laments — its themes of judgment, new covenant build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'mercy' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Compassionate kindness to those in need. In this chapter, it appears in context of judgment. For a first-time reader: think of it as compassionate kindness to those in need, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through judgment and new covenant, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 7 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'Afterward,” says Yahweh, “I will deliver Zedekiah king of Judah, his servants, and the people, even those who are left in this city from the pestilence, from the sword, and from th...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about judgment. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
